narrative:
The model determined that you have a 55% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your undergraduate GPA of 2.70 was the strongest influence. It is noticeably lower than the 3.23 average among accepted students, and this pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. Second, your third-year school decile ranking of 3 was the next most important factor. This is below the 5.8 average of accepted students and pushed the outcome further toward not passing the bar. Third, your upper-middle family income also contributed to the prediction of failure, though its effect was smaller.

Taken together, these academic performance signals outweighed other details such as your LSAT score of 32.5, your plan to attend full-time, and your background as a white female. The system therefore concluded you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam.

What you should do next is focus on strengthening your academic record. Consider retaking courses to raise your GPA, seeking additional study support before the LSAT, or gaining practical legal experience that demonstrates your ability to succeed. With clearer evidence of strong performance, a future application would have a much better chance. (218 words)
